blocks.x: Fire & Blood is less of a novel and more of a fictitious historical account, written by George R. R. Martin. The book details the extensive family history of House Targaryen, one of the most important factions in his novel series A Song of Ice and Fire, which later became the television phenomenon Game of Thrones. Fire & Blood actually served as the basis for a spin-off TV series, known as House of the Dragon.

While fans of the novels would definitely prefer Martin to finish the main series, considering the last installment came out in 2011, Fire & Blood was still a pretty great read. It did a lot for the vast lore of the Seven Kingdoms, detailing lineages a whole three centuries prior to the main event. It's always a pleasure to jump back into the world of Westeros. Plus, those who watch House of the Dragon could easily use this book as a companion piece should they get confused about who's who in the show.

blocks.x: Malazan: Book of the Fallen is considered one of the most quintessential series in modern fantasy literature. The series was started in 1999 by Canadian author Steven Erikson, and it has since expanded to include a large shared universe that multiple authors have contributed to. Deadhouse Landing is one of these books, being part of Malazan's side series, Path to Ascendancy. Only, instead of Erikson being at the helm, Ian Cameron Esslemont is in charge of this one.

It might not be as monumental or epic as some of the other books in the series, especially the ones in the main sequence, but it's still an excellent book filled with a surprising amount of clever humor. Quite a few Malazan side books have come out in the years since this one's release, but this one still stands just a touch above the rest. It's honestly shocking that Malazan hasn't had a TV series yet; the series is so good that it should be a serious contender for a live-action adaptation.
Written by J. R. R. Tolkien

blocks.c: Glorfindel battles a Balrog during the Fall of Gondolin

blocks.x: The Fall of Gondolin is another book that isn't quite a novel, but is more of a historical account. It was written by the one and only J. R. R. Tolkien and is set thousands of years before his critically acclaimed The Lord of the Rings saga. Tolkien died some time ago, so this book was compiled, completed, and posthumously published by his son, Christopher Tolkien. The book consists of three different accounts of the Fall of Gondolin, along with some extra information regarding Tolkien's writings and the lore of Middle-earth.

The story is known as one of the greatest battles of Middle-earth, involving the Dark Lord Morgoth assaulting the hidden Elvish city of Gondolin after its whereabouts are betrayed. The city is assailed by balrogs and orcs, and it is eventually reduced to rubble, its residents forced to evacuate. It's one of the greatest tragedies in Middle-earth — an epic tale of catastrophic devastation. It's also a crucial piece of Tolkien's lore that simply demands to be read. It may not be the best thing Tolkien ever wrote, but it's certainly the best to come out in recent years.

blocks.c: Collider logo
The Stormlight Archive: Oathbringer cover

blocks.x: Oathbringer is the third entry in Brandon Sanderson's ongoing The Stormlight Archive series, which is part of his shared literary universe known as the Cosmere. The premise of the universe is that each series or novel takes place on its own planet within the same galaxy. Each planet has its own unique system of magic. Stormlight takes place on Roshar, a hostile, barren world constantly plagued by highstorms, which are hurricane-like weather events that regularly sweep across the planet. But the highstorms are the least of humanity's worries, as the crustaceous humanoids known as the Listeners have resurrected an ancient evil to destroy the humans. To survive, humanity must refound a magical order known as the Knights Radiant, which has been defunct for over a millennium.

This 1,200-page monster of a book is so epic in all the right ways. There are multiple large-scale battles, thrilling duels to the death, and some genuinely moving moments. It's emotional and rife with character development, and is arguably the best Cosmere book thus far. It's hard to decide what the best part of it is. Is it the unique and interesting world? The genuine moral wisdom found in its pages? Or is it simply a really good story? Actually, it's all of the above. While it might not be Sanderson's best book according to Goodreads, it is certainly in the top three, a spot that it more than deserves. It is one of the most popular and best-rated fantasy books out there, one that earns its spot as the best fantasy novel of the last 10 years.

The series, known as The Burning Kingdoms trilogy, is set in a high fantasy world, though it is inspired by Ancient India. Most fantasy stories go for Medieval European settings, making this one a much-needed breath of fresh air. It also feels much more authentic, with Suri having Indian heritage herself.

The story begins with an empire in chaos and a mysterious disease spreading across the land, prompting magical intervention. But it's not just a story for the sake of telling a story — there is a lesson to be had if you read between the lines. Mainly, the story is about how absolute power can corrupt and how none of that power comes without a monumental cost. It received widespread approval and became a huge hit on social media.

5
'The Burning God' (2020)

Written by R. F. Kuang

Image via Harper Voyager

Author R. F. Kuang has been in a lot of headlines lately, and it's all because of her critically acclaimed novels, which have been blowing up all over social media and sold millions of copies. While her best book is definitely a subject for debate amongst her fans, to this author, her best has to be The Burning God, the third in a stunning and absolutely epic high fantasy trilogy.

Inspired by her Chinese heritage, Kuang created a world based on Imperial China, only containing a lot more magic and monsters. It's actually surprising how deep this book gets. At first, it seems like a romantasy or a YA fantasy, but the content is mature and dark, nestling it comfortably within the grimdark subgenre. Not only are Kuang's books entertaining, but they also contain important social commentary — a result of Kuang's ongoing work in academia. Kuang has achieved quite a lot in just 29 years and has become insanely popular due to her stellar work.

4
'Fire & Blood' (2018)

Written by George R. R. Martin

Image via HBO

Fire & Blood is less of a novel and more of a fictitious historical account, written by George R. R. Martin. The book details the extensive family history of House Targaryen, one of the most important factions in his novel series A Song of Ice and Fire, which later became the television phenomenon Game of Thrones. Fire & Blood actually served as the basis for a spin-off TV series, known as House of the Dragon.

While fans of the novels would definitely prefer Martin to finish the main series, considering the last installment came out in 2011, Fire & Blood was still a pretty great read. It did a lot for the vast lore of the Seven Kingdoms, detailing lineages a whole three centuries prior to the main event. It's always a pleasure to jump back into the world of Westeros. Plus, those who watch House of the Dragon could easily use this book as a companion piece should they get confused about who's who in the show.

3
'Deadhouse Landing' (2017)

Written by Ian Cameron Esslemont

Image via Bantam Books

Malazan: Book of the Fallen is considered one of the most quintessential series in modern fantasy literature. The series was started in 1999 by Canadian author Steven Erikson, and it has since expanded to include a large shared universe that multiple authors have contributed to. Deadhouse Landing is one of these books, being part of Malazan's side series, Path to Ascendancy. Only, instead of Erikson being at the helm, Ian Cameron Esslemont is in charge of this one.

It might not be as monumental or epic as some of the other books in the series, especially the ones in the main sequence, but it's still an excellent book filled with a surprising amount of clever humor. Quite a few Malazan side books have come out in the years since this one's release, but this one still stands just a touch above the rest. It's honestly shocking that Malazan hasn't had a TV series yet; the series is so good that it should be a serious contender for a live-action adaptation.

2
'The Fall of Gondolin' (2018)

Written by J. R. R. Tolkien

Image via Alan Lee/Houghton Miffin

The Fall of Gondolin is another book that isn't quite a novel, but is more of a historical account. It was written by the one and only J. R. R. Tolkien and is set thousands of years before his critically acclaimed The Lord of the Rings saga. Tolkien died some time ago, so this book was compiled, completed, and posthumously published by his son, Christopher Tolkien. The book consists of three different accounts of the Fall of Gondolin, along with some extra information regarding Tolkien's writings and the lore of Middle-earth.

The story is known as one of the greatest battles of Middle-earth, involving the Dark Lord Morgoth assaulting the hidden Elvish city of Gondolin after its whereabouts are betrayed. The city is assailed by balrogs and orcs, and it is eventually reduced to rubble, its residents forced to evacuate. It's one of the greatest tragedies in Middle-earth — an epic tale of catastrophic devastation. It's also a crucial piece of Tolkien's lore that simply demands to be read. It may not be the best thing Tolkien ever wrote, but it's certainly the best to come out in recent years.

1
'Oathbringer' (2017)

Written by Brandon Sanderson

Image via Michael Whelan

Oathbringer is the third entry in Brandon Sanderson's ongoing The Stormlight Archive series, which is part of his shared literary universe known as the Cosmere. The premise of the universe is that each series or novel takes place on its own planet within the same galaxy. Each planet has its own unique system of magic. Stormlight takes place on Roshar, a hostile, barren world constantly plagued by highstorms, which are hurricane-like weather events that regularly sweep across the planet. But the highstorms are the least of humanity's worries, as the crustaceous humanoids known as the Listeners have resurrected an ancient evil to destroy the humans. To survive, humanity must refound a magical order known as the Knights Radiant, which has been defunct for over a millennium.

This 1,200-page monster of a book is so epic in all the right ways. There are multiple large-scale battles, thrilling duels to the death, and some genuinely moving moments. It's emotional and rife with character development, and is arguably the best Cosmere book thus far. It's hard to decide what the best part of it is. Is it the unique and interesting world? The genuine moral wisdom found in its pages? Or is it simply a really good story? Actually, it's all of the above. While it might not be Sanderson's best book according to Goodreads, it is certainly in the top three, a spot that it more than deserves. It is one of the most popular and best-rated fantasy books out there, one that earns its spot as the best fantasy novel of the last 10 years.
